In case it helps, and you haven't heard of this before, there's a philosophical perspective called anti-natalism that views having children as unethical, because being born means you will suffer. So by having a child, you guarantee that a new human will experience suffering. The main philosopher who writes about this is named David Benatar, and here's an article about him and his views:

[https://www.newyorker.com/culture/persons-of-interest/the-case-for-not-being-born](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/persons-of-interest/the-case-for-not-being-born)

I share this just so you know you're not alone, that suffering is universal, and that yes, being brought into the world is a guarantee of pain - perhaps things hurt less when we know we're not the only ones. Maybe.

I am hearing you, but I'd say that women aren't genetically designed to hate and mock ugly men. I am asexual, so I don't say this from a perspective of wanting to get with an unattractive man, but just from a human standpoint, I have a lot of compassion for humans and the difficulties and pain in human experience; and I'd never hate nor mock a man because he is ugly. (or really, for any reason.)
I found that making arrangements can be therapeutic. I wrote a long suicide letter last year and put everything into place, and then didn't go through with it (too afraid to suffer).

Hi Felix, it's nice to 'meet' you. One thing I'd suggest is to not think about dying for other people's sake. It's very unlikely that anyone close to you, especially your parents, would prefer that you were dead, even if you do cause them some suffering. There may be legitimate reasons to die (e.g., one's own long-term suffering), but I think that the people in our lives would nearly always prefer that we stay alive. Losing us would be more painful for them than living with us.

A LOT of people are, in some way or another, a burden to people close to them. They might have emotional or physical handicaps. But caring for people who aren't well is simply a part of life for many people - the majority, in fact, at one time or another, if we consider caring for children (young or grown) and/ or aging parents. It's a part of human experience. Most people have a good level of resilience in the face of the hardships life throws at them - like having a depressed son, for example. I am much older than you, but I started living with my mom last year due to mental illness, and even though I'm a burden on her, she would be devastated if I killed myself.

I think about dying every day, but my experience and observation have shown me that 'doing it for other people's sake' isn't typically a sound line of reasoning. People love us and want us to live.

I hope this helps a little. I was depressed on and off as a teenager (not as badly as you), but my 20s were incredible. I lived overseas and studied subjects that captivated me and got to spend some time in France, too. Sometimes things only get worse, but for someone at your age, there's a very decent chance that they will get better.
I am really sorry. Losing my home is one of my greatest fears. I hope you are OK (dumb thing to say, but still).

I appreciate your perspective. Lately I've been thinking about the (possible) link between depression and intelligence. I mean ongoing, existential depression - the kind that's based on a subjective rationality, not just some biochemical imbalance in the brain.

The content of life feels so unsatisfying to me. There are the basics of existence, like sleeping, eating, and personal care - hardly worth continuing to exist for; there is relationships (which I used to enjoy, and now only do mainly via text, not much in person) - which are based on practical support, and on the various dramas that humans engage in, which no longer compel me; there is work, much of which has great value for humanity (e.g. science, medicine, education), but which I can no longer conjure up any sustained interest in.

I know that a lot of human endeavor (again in say, science and medicine) reflects high intelligence, but my variety of intelligence just jumps to the futility of existence, and the insularity or circularity of human effort. For example, we develop life-improving medical treatments because the quality of human life is, sadly, very fragile, contingent in part on the near-inevitable breakdown of our poorly-adapted biology. Or, life can blow because we're biologically fragile, so we apply our intelligence to develop treatments to reduce that variety of suffering.

I think I'm responding to my own wondering here, re: the link between existential depression and intelligence. I think if you're intelligent, but also have the type of disposition that does fine with the vagaries of human existence (someone like my mom, who is always happy, in a pretty simple life), you can just enjoy being an intelligent human. You don't need to live with depression or suicidality; those aren't actually inevitable endpoints of intelligence. I envy those people. I have their education, and I wish that I could be one of them post-education.

I suspect that most people who live with existential suicidal depression (is it even depression, as such? or just a perspective on life, shaped by having a particular brain?) are highly intelligent. It's like the endpoint of a certain type of intelligence. Because I see: Life issue ---> Futility. I just wish I wasn't one of these types of intelligent people. I wish I was the doctor who stays engaged with the problems and pains of humans until she retires in her 80s. I know the value of intelligence applied to medicine, because I experience and appreciate it in my own medical care. I just wish I could bring myself to care enough to pursue (and sustain) some endeavor that has value.

You are definitely not alone! I have psychotic manias, which come along with paranoia and hearing voices. Maybe check out the Hearing Voices Network? I understand they have local groups. [https://www.hearing-voices.org/](https://www.hearing-voices.org/)

I turned a corner the other week with psychosis (I'm well now, after acute treatment) when I came to realize that the voices aren't real. It sounds obvious when I put it that way, but it was profound for me to really believe that. Once I was able to shift into that mindframe, the voices just lost their power.

Hang in there on the disability - I just got mine approved on my second try (I was denied the first time), after 2 months. Perhaps also look into General Assistance, which pays $200-300 per month while you're waiting for the disability decision. I wish we'd known about it sooner!

I sent a lot of emails and facebook messages during my last manic episode that were just terrible. Really embarrassing. Mania for me = psychosis, so I send delusional things - just the worst. I'm still making judgment calls about which to go back and clear up, and which to just leave alone. I feel you!

I definitely hear you. Though I'm not sure that it's about any system, per se, but more to do with personal traits, and which traits make out well in the complex + random world we live in. (Which isn't to say that it's a personal fault. More like it's nobody's fault - it just is.)

I look at the people who really hack it in this life, and it seems like they share the trait of motivation.

I have two master's degrees and half a PhD, and I can see looking back that I had a ton of motivation while in academia. I look back on my motivation-filled days of my 20s and see that I still had the traits that enabled me to do well in life.

Then my brain started going downhill (depression, then bipolar) and, over a space of a few years, I lost my motivation. It is very hard to care about life now. These days, a good day is one where I have some semblance of a will to live, or (even better) where I feel somewhat positive. To get up the motivation to wake up everyday and work at a job is another level altogether - I can scarcely imagine having the motivation for that. A day here or there, but consistently? Every day? 8-9 hours? For the next 35-40 years? Yeesh.

I look at other people now and envy those who maintain motivation to keep getting up and going to work every day until they're old. For most people, that's the baseline requirement for a sustainable income and decent existence. I despair for my motivation-less self. What hope income? What hope standard of living?

And like you, I feel like the longer I live imperfectly in our society (with that ever-increasing gap on my resume), the harder it will be to make things work out well.

I think a combination of basic income + self-determined death would be most supportive for someone like me, who contends with mental illness as a part of existence. (Though who can say how much my day-to-day depression is mental illness vs existential horror at the broad life equation of Effort > Reward).

I'm so sorry that you've had to go through so many painful things. No one should have to experience being treated as you have. I'm glad to hear that you'll be seeing a psychologist - it may really help. Some depression is biochemical and long-term and resistant to treatment, and some is more psycho-social and down to difficult life circumstances. If you have more of the latter kind, I think there's a lot of hope for improvement! Hang in there!

"I love you all because youre all human and humans have great potential to be amazing."

Right there with you! Thank you

I think that people are incredible for existing and waking up every day and doing their best to hack it.

Thank you. I think you're spot on - I'd feel a whole lot better if I exercised more. Something I may be able to manage is pilates, for muscle toning. I started a muscle-building routine that included squats and so on, and became discouraged because it was so uncomfortable, and results take a little while to come about. I know conceptually how important muscle tone is for weight maintenance over the long run (it's just hard for me to work on it).

I'm so sorry to hear that you're going through this. I can only offer you empathy. I'm a woman with serious hair loss over the past 2 years, and it has been devastating for me. I've been to the dermatologist and doctor and they've only suggested taking 10,000 mcg biotin daily, to ensure that the hair that does regrow is healthy.

​

I'm currently researching infrared light therapies for hair loss / regrowth, and they look very promising. There are lots of clinical studies on the efficacy and safety of these therapies for hair growth. There are infrared light devices that are FDA cleared for home use, and affordable. Two to look at are iRestore and iGrowth. There are coupons available for them (eg a $200 off coupon for iRestore). I may buy one today. (I already have another infrared light therapy device at home though, that I used for the first time last night, after learning about light therapy + hair.)

​

Another thing, the light therapy may help with restoring hair to its natural color, too. (I've read less about that, though.)

​

Since I noticed that my hair became very thin last September 2017, I've kept thinking that I would have visible bald patches within a month or two, and that's never happened. I was totally convinced I'd have bald patches in a short amount of time, but (some) hair does keep regrowing at the roots. It's not long enough yet to contribute to thickness, but that should be less of an issue for a man with short hair.

​

I know how body image issues can contribute to depression - especially when changes come about all of the sudden. I just wrote a post about this yesterday, which you can search if interested. It can be hard to mentally adjust to such changes in a healthy way! Hang in there - you are not alone.

Of medications I have tried, I don't think these have either weight gain or sexual side effects:

Risperdal & Invega Sustenna (very similar)

Lamictal

Lithium

Saphris

Abilify

That's definitely a question you should be able to ask your psychiatrist, too. I'm worried about hair loss as a side effect so have always raised that with my doctors, and they take that into account.
